meta.title: Who really said "You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Maya Angelou really said it — in her interview with Claudia Tate, published 1983. A looser version dates to a 1970 Los Angeles Times interview.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated'?
meta.ogDescription: Verified: Angelou spoke this to Claudia Tate in Black Women Writers at Work (1983). The shared 'We may encounter…' is a pronoun-shifted rewrite.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1928–2014 · American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist
answer.sourceLine: Angelou said this in her interview with Claudia Tate, published in the collection Black Women Writers at Work (Continuum, New York, 1983); Quote Investigator ↗ verified the wording against scans at page 7 of the 1985 Oldcastle Books edition. She had been saying a looser version of it for years — the earliest citation QI found is a Los Angeles Times interview of 16 April 1970, where the line ran “you just must never be defeated.”

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Interview with Maya Angelou, conducted by Claudia Tate — spoken, then transcribed
1983 · Continuum, New York · edited by Claudia Tate
Page 7 of the 1985 Oldcastle Books edition, verified against scans by Quote Investigator

source.excerpt: All my work, my life, everything is about survival. All my work is meant to say, “You may encounter many defeats, but you must not be defeated.” In fact, the encountering may be the very experience which creates the vitality and the power to endure.
trail: 16 April 1970 — the earliest citation on record. The Los Angeles Times reported Angelou’s motives for writing I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, quoting her: “I wanted to say to all girls, ‘You may encounter many defeats, but you just must never be defeated.’” Quote Investigator ↗ cites Maggie Savoy’s article “Faith of Black Woman in a World Full of Conflict,” quote page 8, column 2.

1983 — the wording everyone quotes. Claudia Tate’s interview collection Black Women Writers at Work carries Angelou’s sentence in its now-familiar form. The Internet Archive’s record for the first edition ↗ confirms the publisher and year — New York: Continuum, 1983 — and QI reports verifying the quotation against scans at page 7 of the 1985 Oldcastle Books printing.

1989 to 1999 — how it spread. The Tate interview was reprinted in Conversations with Maya Angelou ↗ (University Press of Mississippi, 1989), which QI cites at page 152, and again in Joanne M. Braxton’s Caged Bird casebook (Oxford University Press, 1999) at page 154. Angelou was still using the line in a 1998 interview about Down in the Delta, the film she directed.

What the reference sites show. Wikiquote’s Maya Angelou page ↗ carries only the altered “We may encounter…” form, filed under “Quotes about Maya Angelou” and footnoted to a link for the poem Phenomenal Woman — so the properly sourced trail for this line is QI’s, not Wikiquote’s.
source.excerptNote: The two-sentence form that later travelled as an epigraph quietly drops a word: a 1995 Abilene Reporter-News article printed “the vitality and power to endure,” where Tate’s transcript has “the vitality and the power to endure” — both wordings are transcribed by Quote Investigator ↗.

source.rightsNote: This is a spoken remark from a book first published in 1983 — far too recent for the public domain in the United States, where protection now reaches works published from 1931 onward. Angelou’s words are licensed by her estate’s entity, Caged Bird Legacy, LLC ↗, and the interview collection itself is Claudia Tate’s, published by Continuum. Even the earliest known version, in a 1970 newspaper interview, is well inside copyright.

author.name: Maya Angelou
author.heading: About Maya Angelou
author.metaLine: 1928–2014 · American memoirist, poet and civil rights activist
author.bio: Maya Angelou (1928–2014) published seven autobiographies, three books of essays and several volumes of poetry, and is credited with plays, films and television work spanning over fifty years. The first memoir, I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings (1969), brought her international recognition; in 1998 she directed the feature film Down in the Delta. Survival was the theme she claimed for the whole body of work — “All my work, my life, everything is about survival” — which is the sentence this quotation was offered to explain.

misattribution.heading: A wording note
misattribution.intro: The attribution here is sound — these are Angelou’s own words, spoken more than once. What drifts is the pronoun and the supposed source.

items.why: The version that dominates sharing is “We may encounter many defeats, but we must not be defeated” — and that is the only form Wikiquote’s Maya Angelou page ↗ carries. But all four wordings using this construction that Quote Investigator reproduces ↗ — 1970, 1983, 1995 and 1998 — read “you,” not “we.” Angelou was addressing someone, not including herself.

items.scope: Sourced to a poem, or to the memoir
items.why: Reference sites and inspirational reprints attach this to her poetry — Wikiquote’s footnote for it is a link to Phenomenal Woman. In fact every citation QI documents ↗ is an interview or a reprint of one. The 1970 newspaper appearance is Angelou talking about why she wrote I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, not a sentence printed inside that book.

The oldest citation reads “You may encounter many defeats, but you just must never be defeated” — two extra words and a different negative. By the Tate interview the sentence had tightened to the version we know. A 1979 Lexington Herald interview shows a third shape entirely: “I believe it may be necessary to encounter many defeats … without being defeated by them” (both transcribed by QI ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Genuinely Maya Angelou, and genuinely in this wording — spoken to Claudia Tate and published in Black Women Writers at Work in 1983, with the same thought on record in her interviews from 1970 onward ↗. Only the pronoun and the alleged source have been altered in transit.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Angelou did not offer this as a stray inspirational line. In the Tate interview it is the sentence she reaches for when asked what her writing is for — she puts survival at the centre of the whole body of work, then supplies this as its message, and immediately complicates it: the defeats are not obstacles to endurance but the thing that manufactures it.

The 1970 version tells you who she had in mind. Explaining I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings to the Los Angeles Times, she said she meant to write it “to black girls, to say ‘you can win’” — and found it had come out addressed to every girl who read it. The second person in “you must not be defeated” is doing real work, which is exactly what the popular “we” rewrite sands off.
context.detailsSummary: The line across three decades of interviews
detailsBody: 1979, Lexington, Kentucky. Asked whether early adversity had embittered her, Angelou drew a distinction between bitterness and anger — bitterness “eats away at you,” anger “purges, and can help you” — and then reached for the defeat idea again in looser form, adding: “Trials shape and mold you.” QI cites Eileen Levy’s interview of 12 April 1979 ↗.

1998, on film. Angelou directed the feature Down in the Delta, and when asked for its central message she gave this sentence verbatim, then glossed it: “When you encounter defeats, you find out who you are, what you can rise up from.” QI cites a Courier-Post interview of 20 December 1998 ↗.

Why the attribution held up. Angelou is one of the most heavily faked names in quotation — unsourced aphorisms attach to her constantly. This one survives scrutiny for the ordinary reason: there is a datable interview behind it, a named interviewer, a publisher, and a page that a researcher has read.
context.pull: All my work, my life, everything is about survival.
